In [[functional analysis]], a '''Markushevich basis''' (sometimes '''M-basis'''<ref name="HušekMill2002">{{cite book |last1=Hušek |first1=Miroslav |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v3_PVdvJek4C&pg=PA182 |title=Recent Progress in General Topology II |last2=Mill |first2=J. van |publisher=Elsevier |year=2002 |isbn=9780444509802 |page=182}}</ref>) is a [[Biorthogonal polynomial|biorthogonal]] system that is both [[Orthonormal basis#Incomplete orthogonal sets|''complete'']] and ''[[Total set|total]]''. Completeness means that the closure of the span is all of the space.<ref name="BierstedtBonet2001">{{cite book|last1=Bierstedt|first1=K.D.|last2=Bonet|first2=J.|last3=Maestre|first3=M.|author4=J. Schmets|title=Recent Progress in Functional Analysis|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=G4t3B7ZHtlgC&pg=PA4|accessdate=28 June 2014|date=2001-09-20|publisher=Elsevier|isbn=9780080515922|page=4}}</ref>

== Definition ==
Conventionally, if the index is <math>i</math>, then it means the [[index set]] is countable. Otherwise, if the index is <math>\alpha</math>, then it means the index set is not necessarily countable.

Let <math>X</math> be [[Banach space]]. A [[biorthogonal system]] <math>\{x_\alpha ; x^*_\alpha\}_{x \in \alpha}</math> in <math>X</math> is a Markushevich basis if <math>\{x_\alpha\}_{x \in \alpha}
</math> is ''complete'' (also called "fundamental"):<math display="block">\overline{\text{span}}\{x_\alpha \} = X</math>and <math>\{x^*_\alpha\}_{x \in \alpha}
</math> is ''total'': it [[Separating set|separates the points]] of <math>X</math>. Totality is equivalently stated as <math display="inline">\overline{\text{span}}\{x^*_\alpha \} = X^*</math> where the closure is taken under the [[weak-star topology]].  

A Markushevich basis is '''shrinking''' iff we further have <math display="inline">\overline{\text{span}}\{x^*_\alpha \} = X^*</math> under the topology induced by the [[operator norm]] on <math>X^*</math>.  

A Markushevich basis is '''bounded''' iff <math>\sup_\alpha \|x_\alpha \| \|x^*_\alpha\| < \infty</math>.  

A Markushevich basis <math display="inline">\left\{x_n ; x_n^*\right\}_{n=1}^{\infty} \subset X \times X^*</math> is '''strong''' iff <math display="inline">x \in \overline{\operatorname{span}}\left\{\left\langle x, x_n^*\right\rangle x_n\right\}_{n=1}^{\infty}</math> for all <math display="inline">x \in X</math>.


Since <math>x^*_\alpha(x_\alpha) = 1</math>, we always have the lower bound <math>\|x_\alpha \| \|x^*_\alpha\| \geq 1</math>, and therefore <math>\sup_i \|x_i \| \|x^*_i\| \in [1, \infty]</math>.  

If <math>\sup_\alpha \|x_\alpha \| \|x^*_\alpha\| = 1</math>, then we can simply scale both so that <math>\|x_\alpha\| = \|x^*_\alpha\| = 1</math> for all <math>\alpha</math>. This special case of the Markushevich basis is called an [[Auerbach basis|'''Auerbach basis''']]. [[Auerbach's lemma]] states that any finite-dimensional Banach space has an Auerbach basis.

== Properties ==
In a [[separable space]], Markushevich bases exist and in great abundance. Any spanning set and separating functionals can be made into a Markushevich basis by an inductive process similar to a [[Gram–Schmidt process]]:

{{Math theorem|name=Theorem|note=<ref name="Fabian2001" />{{Reference page|location=Theorem 4.59}}|math_statement= Let <math display="inline">X</math> be a separable Banach space. If <math display="inline">\left\{z_i\right\}_i \subset X</math> satisfies <math display="inline">\overline{\operatorname{span}}\left\{z_i\right\}_i=X</math> and <math display="inline">\left\{g_i\right\}_i \subset X^*</math> separates points of <math display="inline">X</math>, then there is a Markushevich basis <math display="inline">\left\{x_i ; x^*_i\right\}</math> of <math display="inline">X</math> such that <math display="inline">\operatorname{span}\left\{x_i\right\}=\operatorname{span}\left\{z_i\right\}</math> and <math display="inline">\operatorname{span}\left\{x^*_i\right\}=\operatorname{span}\left\{g_i\right\}</math>.
}}

{{hidden begin|style=width:100%|ta1=center|border=1px #aaa solid|title=Proof}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof= 

Define <math display="inline">x_1=z_1</math> and <math display="inline">x^*_1=g_{k_1} / g_{k_1}\left(z_1\right)</math>, where <math display="inline">k_1 \in \mathbb{N}</math> is such that <math display="inline">g_{k_1}\left(z_1\right) \neq 0</math>. Then find the smallest integer <math display="inline">h_2</math> such that <math display="inline">g_{h_2} \notin \operatorname{span}\left\{x^*_1\right\}</math>. Define <math display="inline">x^*_2=g_{h_2}-g_{h_2}\left(x_1\right) x^*_1</math>. Find an index <math display="inline">k_2</math> such that <math display="inline">x^*_2\left(z_{k_2}\right) \neq 0</math>, and set <math display="inline">x_2=\left(z_{k_2}-\right. \left.x^*_1\left(z_{k_2}\right) x_1\right) / x^*_2\left(z_{k_2}\right)</math>. Let <math display="inline">h_3</math> be the smallest integer such that <math display="inline">z_{h_3} \notin \operatorname{span}\left\{x_1, x_2\right\}</math>. Put <math display="inline">x_3=z_{h_3}-x^*_1\left(z_{h_3}\right) x_1-x^*_2\left(z_{h_3}\right) x_2</math> and <math display="inline">x^*_3=\left(g_{k_3}-g_{k_3}\left(x_1\right) x^*_1-g_{k_3}\left(x_2\right) x^*_2\right) / g_{k_3}\left(x_3\right)</math>, where <math display="inline">k_3</math> is an index such that <math display="inline">g_{k_3}\left(x_3\right) \neq 0</math>. Continue by induction. At the step <math display="inline">2 n</math> we construct <math display="inline">x^*_{2 n}</math> first, at the step <math display="inline">2 n+1</math> we start by constructing <math display="inline">x_{2 n+1}</math>. It follows that <math display="inline">\operatorname{span}\left\{z_i\right\}_1^n \subset \operatorname{span}\left\{x_i\right\}_1^{2 n}</math> and <math display="inline">\operatorname{span}\left\{g_i\right\}_1^n \subset \operatorname{span}\left\{x^*_i\right\}_1^{2 n}</math>. Clearly <math display="inline">x^*_i\left(x_j\right)=\delta_{i j}</math>, <math display="inline">\operatorname{span}\left\{x_i\right\} \subset \operatorname{span}\left\{z_i\right\}</math> and <math display="inline">\operatorname{span}\left\{x^*_i\right\} \subset \operatorname{span}\left\{g_i\right\}</math>.
}}{{hidden end}} 

The above construction, however, does not guarantee that the constructed basis is bounded. 

It is known currently that for every separable Banach space, for any <math>\epsilon > 0</math>, there exists a Markushevich basis, such that <math>\sup_i \|x_i\| \|x^*_i \| < 1 + \epsilon</math>.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|location=Theorem 1.27}} However, it is an [[open problem]] whether the lower limit is reachable. That is, whether every separable Banach space has a Markushevich basis where <math>\|x_i \| \|x^*_i\| = 1</math> for all <math>i</math>. That is, whether every separable Banach space has an Auerbach basis.<ref name="Fabian2001">{{cite book |author=Fabian |first=Marián&nbsp;J. |url=https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/978-1-4419-7515-7.pdf |title=Banach Space Theory: The Basis for Linear and Nonlinear Analysis |last2=Habala |first2=Petr |last3=Hájek |first3=Petr |last4=Montesinos&nbsp;Santalucía |first4=Vicente |last5=Zizler |first5=Václav |date=2011 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-1-4419-7515-7 |location=New York |pages=216–218 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4419-7515-7}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite book |last1=Hájek |first1=Petr |title=Biorthogonal Systems in Banach Spaces |last2=Montesinos Santalucía |first2=Vicente |last3=Vanderwerff |first3=Jon |last4=Zizler |first4=Václav |date=2007 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-0-387-68914-2 |edition=1st |series=CMS Books in Mathematics |location=New York, NY |doi=10.1007/978-0-387-68915-9}}</ref>

Similarly, any Markushevich basis of a closed subspace can be extended:

{{Math theorem|name=Theorem|note=<ref name="Fabian2001" />{{Reference page|location=Theorem 4.60}}|math_statement= Let <math display="inline">Z</math> be a closed subspace of a separable Banach space <math display="inline">X</math>. Any Markushevich basis <math display="inline">\{x_i; x^*_i\}</math> of <math display="inline">Z</math> can be extended to a Markushevich basis of <math display="inline">X</math>.
}}

Every separable Banach space admits an M-basis that is not strong.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|location=Proposition 1.34}} Every separable Banach space admits an M-basis that is strong.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|location=Theorem 1.36}}

== Examples ==
Any Markushevich basis <math>\{x_i ; x_i^*\}_{x \in i}</math> of a separable Banach space can be converted to an unbounded Markushevich basis:<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=10}}<math display="block">\begin{array}{ll}
v_{2 n-1}:=x_{2 n-1}, & v_{2 n}:=x_{2 n-1}+\frac{1}{2 n} x_{2 n} \\
v_{2 n-1}^*:=x_{2 n-1}^*-2 n x_{2 n}^*, & v_{2 n}^*:=2 n x_{2 n}^*
\end{array}</math>Every [[Schauder basis]] of a Banach space is also a Markushevich basis; the converse is not true in general. An example of a Markushevich basis that is not a Schauder basis is the sequence <math display=block>\{e^{2 i \pi n t}\}_{n \isin \mathbb{Z}}\quad\quad\quad(\text{ordered }n=0,\pm1,\pm2,\dots)</math> in the subspace <math>\tilde{C}[0,1]</math> of [[continuous function]]s from <math>[0,1]</math> to the [[complex number]]s that have equal values on the boundary, under the [[Uniform norm|supremum norm]].  The computation of a Fourier coefficient is continuous and the span dense in <math>\tilde{C}[0,1]</math>; thus for any <math>f\in\tilde{C}[0,1]</math>, there exists a sequence <math display="block">\sum_{|n|<N}{\alpha_{N,n}e^{2\pi int}}\to f\text{.}</math>But if <math>f=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}{\alpha_ne^{2\pi nit}}</math>, then for a fixed <math>n</math> the coefficients <math>\{\alpha_{N,n}\}_N</math> must converge, and there are functions for which they do not.<ref name=Fabian2001 /><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Albiac |first1=Fernando |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-319-31557-7 |title=Topics in Banach Space Theory |last2=Kalton |first2=Nigel&nbsp;J. |publisher=Springer |year=2006 |isbn=978-3-319-31557-7 |edition=2nd |series=GTM 233 |location=Switzerland |publication-date=2016 |pages=9–10 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-31557-7}}</ref>

The [[sequence space]] <math>l^\infty</math> admits no Markushevich basis, because it is both [[Grothendieck space|Grothendieck]] and [[reflexive space|irreflexive]].  But any separable space (such as <math>l^1</math>) has dual (resp. <math>l^\infty</math>) complemented in a space admitting a Markushevich basis.<ref name=Fabian2001 />
